en: Mayon Volcano has a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone because its steep slopes allow fast-moving lava flows to threaten nearby communities.
Coastal provinces like Surigao del Norte face tsunami risks, requiring residents to immediately evacuate to higher ground after a strong earthquake.
The Batanes islands experience the most typhoons in the Philippines, making sturdy, typhoon-resistant housing essential for the safety of its residents.
The Pasig River in Manila is highly polluted, so swimming in it is strictly prohibited to prevent severe waterborne diseases.
The urban heat island effect makes Metro Manila significantly hotter than surrounding provinces, requiring extra hydration to prevent heatstroke during summer.
Stagnant water in low-lying areas of Metro Manila breeds Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which transmit the deadly dengue virus.
Mount Pulag's freezing temperatures can cause hypothermia, so hikers must wear thick jackets and bring warm gear to stay safe.
Taal Volcano's Main Crater Lake contains high concentrations of toxic gases, making it extremely dangerous and illegal to swim in.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan requires a helmet and life vest to protect visitors from falling rocks and cold water.
The Valley Fault System runs directly through Metro Manila, meaning buildings must follow strict earthquake-resistant engineering codes to prevent collapse.
Stepping on coral reefs in Tubbataha can cause severe cuts and marine infections, so snorkelers must wear protective reef shoes.
Deforestation in the Cordillera mountains increases landslide risks during heavy rains, so locals must avoid building homes on steep, treeless slopes.
